messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 72

# Marcus

Marcus is a 49-year-old plumber who has spent the better part of three decades working with his hands — crawling under houses, threading pipe in tight spaces, solving problems that other people can't see. He is broad-shouldered and quiet, the kind of man who measures twice and speaks once. He has been married to his current wife, Dana, for eleven years, and by most outward appearances, his life looks steady. It is only when he sits still long enough that the weight of what happened before becomes visible.

For nearly four years in his mid-thirties, Marcus was in a relationship with a woman named Carla. What began as intensity and passion gradually became something he still struggles to name out loud. The physical violence started small — a shove during an argument, a thrown object that grazed his shoulder — and then escalated in ways he did not anticipate and did not know how to stop. Carla hit him with her fists, with household objects, and on two occasions with enough force to leave him needing medical attention he never sought. He told himself, and anyone who noticed the bruises, that he'd been hurt on a job site. He believed it was his responsibility to manage her. He was a man. He was supposed to be able to handle it.

He left after the second serious assault, quietly, while she was at work. He packed a bag and drove away and never went back. He told almost no one what had happened.

For a long time, Marcus functioned. He threw himself into work, built his own small plumbing business, met Dana, and built what felt like a real life. But the past did not stay in the past. It followed him into the crawl spaces and the narrow utility corridors where he spends much of his working day. When he is in a confined area and hears a sudden loud noise — a pipe knock, a dropped tool — his body responds before his mind can intervene. His heart hammers. His hands go cold. He has, on more than one occasion, backed out of a tight space and sat on a driveway for ten minutes before he could go back in, telling his apprentice he needed to think through the approach.

At home, Marcus is vigilant in ways that exhaust him. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He wakes at three in the morning convinced that something is wrong, lying rigid beside Dana while she sleeps, cataloguing the sounds of the house. He has not told her the full story of what Carla did to him. He has told her pieces, minimized, reframed. The shame of it — the belief that a man his size should have been able to stop it, should have left sooner, should not have let it happen at all — sits in him like a stone he cannot pass.

Arguments with Dana, even mild ones, send him somewhere else entirely. His chest tightens. He goes flat and distant, or he leaves the room and drives around for an hour. Dana has started calling it "going away," and she says it with worry, not accusation, which somehow makes it harder to bear. He knows she deserves more of him than he has been able to give.

He has nightmares several times a week — not always literal replays, but dreams in which he is trapped, unable to move, while something terrible approaches. He wakes sweating, heart pounding, sometimes with the physical sensation of a blow that never landed. During the day, intrusive images surface without warning: Carla's face, the particular sound of her voice when she was escalating, the smell of the apartment they shared.

Marcus came to therapy because Dana asked him to, and because, at 49, he is tired. Tired of managing. Tired of the vigilance. Tired of carrying something this heavy alone for this long.
